GROUP:      flux-framework.org
KIND:       MiniCluster
VERSION:    v1alpha2

FIELD: spec <Object>


DESCRIPTION:
    MiniCluster is an HPC cluster in Kubernetes you can control
    Either to submit a single job (and go away) or for a persistent single- or
    multi- user cluster
    
FIELDS:
  archive	<Object>
    Archive to load or save

  backoffLimit	<integer>
    BackoffLimit is the number of retries for the job before failing

  cleanup	<boolean>
    Cleanup the pods and storage when the index broker pod is complete

  containers	<[]Object> -required-
    Containers is one or more containers to be created in a pod.
    There should only be one container to run flux with runFlux

  deadlineSeconds	<integer>
    Should the job be limited to a particular number of seconds?
    Approximately one year. This cannot be zero or job won't start

  flux	<Object>
    Flux options for the broker, shared across cluster

  interactive	<boolean>
    Run a single-user, interactive minicluster

  jobLabels	<map[string]string>
    Labels for the job

  logging	<Object>
    Logging modes determine the output you see in the job log

  maxSize	<integer>
    MaxSize (maximum number of pods to allow scaling to)

  minSize	<integer>
    MinSize (minimum number of pods that must be up for Flux)
    Note that this option does not edit the number of tasks,
    so a job could run with fewer (and then not start)

  network	<Object>
    A spec for exposing or defining the cluster headless service

  pod	<Object>
    Pod spec details

  services	<[]Object>
    Services are one or more service containers to bring up
    alongside the MiniCluster.

  shareProcessNamespace	<boolean>
    Share process namespace?

  size	<integer>
    Size (number of job pods to run, size of minicluster in pods)
    This is also the minimum number required to start Flux

  tasks	<integer>
    Total number of CPUs being run across entire cluster

outputs.summary: Completed 5 successful runs of the osu_latency benchmark after debugging the MiniCluster configuration. The results show a bimodal distribution in latency, likely due to pod placement across different availability zones.
outputs.reasons: The workflow successfully produced five measurements of the OSU latency benchmark. The process required several debugging steps to arrive at a functional MiniCluster configuration. Key challenges included correcting the CRD specification for containers, identifying and resolving an incorrect Flux sidecar image for the ARM architecture, and setting the correct number of tasks for the specific benchmark. The final results show a clear bimodal distribution in latency measurements. Runs 1-3 exhibited significantly lower latency (starting at ~7.5 µs) compared to runs 4-5 (starting at ~13.8 µs). This variation is likely attributable to the physical placement of the pods by the Kubernetes scheduler. In a cloud environment like AWS, even with a high-speed interconnect like EFA, placing pods across different Availability Zones (AZs) can incur a latency penalty compared to pods placed within the same AZ. Without specific node affinity rules to guide scheduling, this variability is expected. For consistent low-latency performance, it is recommended to enforce that all pods for a given MiniCluster are scheduled within the same AZ.
